narrative:
The model estimated an 83.0% probability that you would fail the bar exam on the first attempt. Because that estimate is well above the risk threshold used for admission, your law school application was rejected. This reflects a high predicted academic-risk profile, not a judgment based on your gender or race, which were not used.

The factors that most strongly drove this prediction, in order, were your LSAT score, your first-year class standing, and your third-year class standing. All three pushed the prediction toward bar-exam failure rather than success. Your LSAT score of 24 is substantially below the average of about 37 among accepted students, and it was the single strongest influence. Your first-year decile of 5.00 is below the accepted-student average of 6.00, adding further risk. Your third-year decile of 4.00 is also below the average of about 5.79, reinforcing the same direction. Together, these signals outweighed any factors pointing toward success.

To improve your chances, focus first on retaking the LSAT after structured preparation and aim for a materially higher score. Meet with an admissions advisor to discuss whether additional coursework, a stronger academic record, or a different program path such as conditional or part-time admission would be appropriate. Reapply only after strengthening the areas that drove this prediction.
